canonicalExplanation.summary: Handle forms at the **form**, not the button: `form.addEventListener("submit", ...)` catches every way of submitting, including pressing Enter in a field. Read values by name with `new FormData(form)`. **Validate first**, and call `event.preventDefault()` because you're sending the data yourself with fetch. While the request runs, **disable the submit button** and show status in an `aria-live` region so screen-reader users hear it. On an error, put a message next to the field, mark it `aria-invalid="true"`, and move focus to it. JavaScript validation is an **enhancement**: the HTML `required` and `type` attributes still work if the script fails.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A sign-up page listens for clicks on the Join button. Then a second "Join with invite" button and an auto-submit script (`form.requestSubmit()`) are added, and both skip all the checks. Impatient double-clicks also create two accounts. A submit listener prevents navigation only after validation and disables duplicate requests while showing status. In this lesson you'll implement client validation as enhancement and verify keyboard focus and error announcement behavior.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Scope, closures and modules** module, the **Semantic multi-page site**, **Event propagation and delegation** (submit bubbles to the form), and **Native constraints and error semantics** (required, type=email and labels).

sections.heading: The rule: submit on the form, validate, then lock
Where does focus go?

includes: Handle submit at the form, read FormData, validate and prevent duplicate requests.
Announce errors and status accessibly and manage focus.
excludes: Server-side validation (always required too, covered in the backend track).

outcomes: Implement client validation as enhancement and verify keyboard focus and error announcement behavior.

examples.title: The sign-up form that submitted twice
examples.situation: A submit listener prevents navigation only after validation and disables duplicate requests while showing status.
walkthrough: **Move the listener:** switch from a button click listener to `form.addEventListener("submit", ...)`, so every submit button and requestSubmit() are caught too.
**Validate first:** a bad email sets aria-invalid, writes the message to the live region, and focuses the field.
**Lock while sending:** the handler disables the button and shows "Creating your account..."; a double-click will send only one request.
examples.result: Every submission is validated, keyboard users hear errors, and only one account is created per sign-up.

examples.title: The silent error message
examples.situation: An error message is added as red text under the field, but screen-reader users submit the form and hear nothing.
walkthrough: The message appears visually but isn't announced.
Focus stays on the button, so nothing points them to the problem.
Fix: write the message into an aria-live region, set aria-invalid on the field, and call field.focus().
examples.result: Screen-reader users hear the error and land on the field that needs fixing.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Handling the submit button's click is equivalent to handling every form submission.
misconceptions.correction: A form can be submitted without clicking that button, for example by another submit button or form.requestSubmit(). The submit event on the form is the reliable boundary for validation.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The sign-up form that submitted twice", which listener catches every submission?

analogy.example: A form submit handler is like **a checkout desk**: every customer must pass it no matter which door they came in (click or Enter). The cashier checks the basket first, points at the problem item, and puts up a "processing" sign so the same customer can't pay twice.
limitations: Desks don't talk to screen readers; aria-live does.
The shop's own security (HTML validation) still works if the cashier is away.

artifact: learner fixes email and submits again

steps.explanation: The submit listener catches Enter and prevents navigation.
Validation fails, so the error is announced and focus moves.
The handler disables duplicate requests while showing status.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a validated submission. Step 1, Submit: event is submit; navigation is prevented. The submit listener catches Enter and prevents navigation. Step 2, Invalid: aria-invalid is true; focus is email field; status is error announced. Validation fails, so the error is announced and focus moves. Step 3, Valid: button.disabled is true; requests sent is 1. The handler disables duplicate requests while showing status.

nearTransfer.prompt: A feedback form needs a message of at least 10 characters. Write the submit handler: read FormData, validate, announce the error, focus the textarea, or show "Thanks!".
expectedEvidence: Short messages focus the textarea with aria-invalid.

farTransfer.prompt: Enhance a plain HTML login form with client validation, a disabled-while-sending button and live status. Test keyboard-only submission, the error announcement, and that it still works without JavaScript.
expectedEvidence: Tests for focus, aria-invalid and one request.

remediation.explanation: Checklist per form: **submit on form? FormData? validate before sending? button disabled during the request? error in aria-live, aria-invalid set, focus moved?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The silent error message".

recap.summary: To implement client validation as enhancement, listen for submit on the form, read named controls with FormData, validate before sending, prevent navigation, disable the button to block duplicates, and announce status and errors with aria-live, aria-invalid and focus, keeping native HTML validation as the baseline.
